body:
Understanding rocks and minerals

The solid outer part of the Earth contains rocks of different origins, compositions and physical properties. These rocks provide the material from which landforms and soils develop. They also contain many of the natural resources used in agriculture, construction, manufacturing and energy production.

A mineral is a naturally occurring, generally inorganic solid with an orderly internal atomic structure and a characteristic chemical composition. A rock is a naturally occurring mass composed of 1 or more minerals or other geological materials.

Quartz, feldspar, mica and calcite are minerals. Granite, basalt, sandstone and marble are rocks. Granite usually contains several minerals, principally quartz and feldspar, together with minerals such as mica. Quartzite, on the other hand, may consist predominantly of a single mineral, quartz.

Unlike an individual mineral, a rock does not necessarily have a fixed chemical composition. Different samples of granite, for example, may contain different proportions of their constituent minerals.

The scientific study of minerals is called mineralogy, while the study of the composition, origin, structure and transformation of rocks is called petrology.

Major elements and rock-forming minerals

Oxygen and silicon are the 2 most abundant elements by mass in the Earth's crust. Other major crustal elements include aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium.

Oxygen and silicon combine with each other and with other elements to form silicate minerals. Silicates constitute the dominant group of rock-forming minerals in the Earth's crust. Feldspar is the most abundant mineral group in the crust, while quartz is another very common rock-forming mineral.

MineralCharacteristicOccurrence or use
FeldsparAluminium-bearing silicate mineralsGranite, glass and ceramics
QuartzSilicon dioxide; relatively hardGranite, sandstone, glass and electronics
MicaSplits into thin sheetsGranite, schist and electrical insulation
PyroxeneCommonly contains iron and magnesiumBasalt and gabbro
AmphiboleComplex silicate mineral groupVarious igneous and metamorphic rocks
OlivineIron-magnesium silicateMany mafic and ultramafic rocks
CalciteCalcium carbonateLimestone and marble

Minerals composed of a single element

Many minerals are chemical compounds containing multiple elements. However, some occur naturally as individual elements. Gold, silver, native copper, sulphur, diamond and graphite are examples.

Diamond and graphite are both composed of carbon, but their atoms are arranged differently. Diamond is extremely hard, whereas graphite is soft. This illustrates how internal atomic structure influences mineral properties.

The 3 major rock families

Rocks are classified primarily according to their mode of formation, rather than their colour, hardness or economic value.

  • Igneous rocks: Form when molten rock cools and solidifies.
  • Sedimentary rocks: Form from accumulated sediments, chemical precipitation or biological material.
  • Metamorphic rocks: Form when existing rocks undergo changes under heat, pressure or chemically active fluids without completely melting.

Prelims focus

  • Oxygen is the most abundant element by mass in the Earth's crust, followed by silicon.
  • Feldspar is the most abundant crustal mineral group.
  • Quartz consists of silicon dioxide.
  • Petrology studies rocks; mineralogy studies minerals.
  • Diamond and graphite have the same elemental composition but different atomic structures.
  • Trap: Granite is a rock, whereas quartz is a mineral.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 8-10; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2019-2020 reprint, Chapter 5, pp. 40-42, online copy consulted where the project text was unreadable; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 36-40, online copy; US Geological Survey, What Is the Difference Between a Rock and a Mineral?; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Navnirman, July-December 1985. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Rocks, Minerals and the Composition of the Earth's Crust

body:
How minerals are identified

Minerals possess characteristic physical properties because their atoms are arranged in particular ways and are joined by chemical bonds of different strengths. These properties help distinguish minerals that may otherwise look similar.

Important identifying properties

PropertyMeaning
Crystal formExternal geometrical shape reflecting internal atomic arrangement
ColourVisible colour of a mineral, sometimes affected by impurities
StreakColour of a mineral in powdered form
LustreAppearance of light reflected from the mineral surface
HardnessResistance to scratching
CleavageTendency to split along definite planes
FractureBreaking along surfaces other than cleavage planes
Specific gravityRatio of the density of a mineral to that of water
TransparencyExtent to which light passes through a mineral

Colour alone is not always reliable for identifying a mineral. Quartz may occur in several colours because of impurities or variations in its crystal structure. Different minerals may also have a similar external colour but produce different streaks.

Cleavage and fracture

A mineral exhibits cleavage when it breaks preferentially along planes of weakness within its crystal structure. Mica has excellent cleavage in 1 direction and therefore separates into thin sheets.

Quartz does not have prominent cleavage. It commonly breaks along curved, shell-like surfaces known as conchoidal fracture.

Mohs scale of mineral hardness

The Mohs scale arranges 10 reference minerals in increasing order of scratch hardness. A mineral with a higher hardness can generally scratch a mineral with a lower hardness.

HardnessReference mineral
1Talc
2Gypsum
3Calcite
4Fluorite
5Apatite
6Orthoclase feldspar
7Quartz
8Topaz
9Corundum
10Diamond

A human fingernail has an approximate hardness of 2.5, while ordinary glass has a hardness of about 5.5. Therefore, quartz can generally scratch ordinary glass, whereas calcite cannot.

The Mohs scale is a relative, non-linear scale. A mineral with hardness 10 is not merely twice as hard as a mineral with hardness 5. Hardness also does not mean resistance to every kind of breakage: a hard mineral may still fracture or cleave.

Other useful distinctions

Metallic lustre does not necessarily establish that a mineral is a commercially useful metal ore. Likewise, the hardness of a rock depends on its constituent minerals, their arrangement and the strength with which they are held together.

Prelims focus

  • Talc has hardness 1; diamond has hardness 10.
  • Calcite, feldspar and quartz have hardness values of 3, 6 and 7 respectively.
  • Corundum is harder than topaz but softer than diamond.
  • Streak refers to powdered colour, not necessarily external colour.
  • Mica exhibits excellent cleavage; quartz commonly exhibits conchoidal fracture.
  • Trap: Mineral hardness measures resistance to scratching, not resistance to all forms of breakage.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2019-2020 reprint, Chapter 5, pp. 40-41; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, Rocks, Minerals and Soil; US Geological Survey, Minerals 101 and educational resources on mineral identification. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Physical Properties and Identification of Minerals

body:
Formation from molten material

Igneous rocks originate when molten rock cools and becomes solid. Molten material below the Earth's surface is called magma. When magma reaches the surface through a volcanic eruption or fissure, the erupted molten material is called lava.

As magma or lava cools, minerals crystallise. The resulting rock depends on the composition of the molten material, the rate of cooling and the conditions under which solidification occurs.

Igneous rocks are traditionally called primary rocks because they form directly from molten material and can provide the parent material for sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

Classification according to place of formation

Intrusive igneous rocks

When magma solidifies beneath the Earth's surface, it forms intrusive igneous rocks. Magma at considerable depth usually cools slowly because the surrounding rocks limit heat loss. The mineral crystals consequently have more time to grow, producing a generally coarse-grained texture.

Deep-seated intrusive rocks are also called plutonic rocks. Granite and gabbro are common examples. Intrusive rocks formed at relatively shallow depths may have intermediate grain sizes and are traditionally termed hypabyssal rocks.

Extrusive igneous rocks

When lava solidifies at or near the surface, it generally loses heat rapidly. Mineral crystals remain small, producing a fine-grained rock. Basalt and rhyolite are common examples of extrusive or volcanic rocks.

Exceptionally rapid cooling may prevent appreciable crystal growth and produce volcanic glass, such as obsidian. Escaping or trapped gases may produce cavities in volcanic rocks. Pumice is a highly porous volcanic rock formed from gas-rich magma.

FeatureIntrusiveExtrusive
FormationBelow the surfaceAt or near the surface
Typical coolingSlowRapid
Typical crystalsLargeSmall or absent
ExamplesGranite, gabbroBasalt, rhyolite

Classification according to composition

Igneous rocks also differ in their silica content and mineral composition.

  • Felsic rocks: Relatively rich in silica and commonly contain quartz and feldspar. They are often light-coloured. Granite and rhyolite are examples.
  • Mafic rocks: Relatively rich in iron and magnesium-bearing minerals and lower in silica than felsic rocks. They are commonly dark-coloured. Basalt and gabbro are examples.

Granite and rhyolite have broadly similar felsic compositions but different cooling histories. Similarly, gabbro and basalt have broadly similar mafic compositions but differ in their typical grain sizes.

Continental crust contains abundant granitic and related rocks, whereas basalt and gabbro are important constituents of oceanic crust.

Intrusive structures: dykes and sills

Magma may enter cracks or spaces within older rocks before solidifying. A dyke cuts across the existing layers of rock, whereas a sill is intruded broadly parallel to those layers. Both are intrusive igneous structures.

The Deccan Traps and Gujarat

The Deccan Traps originated from extensive volcanic eruptions that spread successive sheets of predominantly basaltic lava over parts of western and central India.

These lava flows, together with later weathering and erosion, produced characteristic stepped landscapes. The term trap is derived from a word meaning stairs or steps.

In Gujarat, Deccan Trap rocks occur extensively in Saurashtra and eastern parts of South Gujarat. Successive lava flows contribute to the stepped relief of several hill regions. The weathering of basaltic parent material has also contributed to the development of black soils in the Deccan region, including parts of Gujarat.

Prelims focus

  • Igneous rocks are known as primary rocks.
  • Granite and gabbro are intrusive; basalt and rhyolite are extrusive.
  • Slow cooling generally produces larger crystals.
  • Granite is felsic; basalt is mafic.
  • The Deccan Traps consist predominantly of basaltic lava flows.
  • Trap: The word intrusive describes formation below the surface, even if the rock later becomes exposed by erosion.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 8-9; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2019-2020 reprint, Chapter 5, pp. 41-42; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 36-37; US Geological Survey, Collecting Rocks, Types of Rocks; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Navnirman, July-December 1985, pp. 1-2. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Igneous Rocks: Formation, Types and the Deccan Traps

body:
Formation of sedimentary rocks

When rocks are exposed at the Earth's surface, weathering breaks them down physically or alters them chemically. The resulting fragments and dissolved substances may be transported by water, wind, glaciers and gravity.

When transporting agents lose their capacity to carry material, sediments accumulate in places such as river valleys, lakes, deserts, coastal areas and ocean basins. Burial beneath additional deposits may eventually convert loose sediments into solid rock.

Lithification is the conversion of unconsolidated sediment into coherent sedimentary rock, commonly through compaction and cementation.

Compaction and cementation

Compaction occurs when the weight of overlying deposits compresses the sediments, reducing the spaces between their particles. Cementation occurs when dissolved minerals, such as silica or calcium carbonate, precipitate within these spaces and bind the particles together.

Not all sedimentary rocks originate from transported rock fragments. Some form directly through chemical precipitation, while others originate largely from biological remains.

Major types of sedimentary rocks

Mechanically formed or clastic sedimentary rocks

These originate from fragments of pre-existing rocks or minerals. They are classified partly according to the size and characteristics of the particles from which they form.

RockConstituent materialCharacteristic
ConglomerateGravel and pebblesRounded coarse fragments
BrecciaCoarse rock fragmentsAngular fragments
SandstoneSand-sized particlesVisible or recognisable sand grains
SiltstoneSilt-sized particlesFiner than sandstone
ShaleClay and fine siltCommonly splits into thin layers

Chemically formed sedimentary rocks

These form when substances dissolved in water precipitate as solid minerals. For example, evaporation of saline water may produce deposits of rock salt and gypsum. Rocks produced by evaporation are called evaporites.

Some varieties of limestone also form through direct precipitation of calcium carbonate from water.

Biologically or organically formed sedimentary rocks

Biological processes produce many sedimentary deposits. The shells and skeletons of marine organisms may accumulate and form limestone or chalk. Coal develops from buried plant material that undergoes progressive transformation under burial conditions.

Limestone does not belong exclusively to a single subdivision of sedimentary rocks. It may originate through biological accumulation, chemical precipitation or the accumulation of carbonate fragments.

Stratification and fossils

Sedimentary deposits frequently accumulate in successive layers called beds or strata. This arrangement is known as stratification or bedding.

In a sequence of sedimentary layers that has not been overturned, the lower layers are generally older than the upper layers. This relationship is called the principle of superposition.

Sedimentary rocks are particularly important for preserving fossils, including preserved remains, impressions and traces of ancient organisms. They provide evidence of earlier environments and the history of life.

Fossils are most commonly found in sedimentary rocks because sediment deposition and burial can preserve biological material. The high temperatures associated with magma and the conditions of intense metamorphism usually destroy or alter such evidence.

Indian and Gujarat examples

The Red Fort in Delhi is famous for its use of red sandstone. Sandstone is also an important construction material in other parts of India.

Kachchh contains extensive sedimentary rock formations, including sandstone, shale and fossil-bearing limestone. These formations record earlier geological environments, including periods of marine sedimentation. The region also contains volcanic rocks, demonstrating that one geographical region can contain more than one rock family.

Prelims focus

  • Lithification commonly involves compaction and cementation.
  • Conglomerate contains rounded fragments; sedimentary breccia contains angular fragments.
  • Rock salt and gypsum are common evaporite deposits.
  • Coal is an organic sedimentary rock.
  • Fossils occur most commonly in sedimentary rocks.
  • Trap: Limestone is not exclusively of chemical or biological origin; both modes are possible.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 8-9; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2019-2020 reprint, Chapter 5, p. 42; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6; US Geological Survey, Collecting Rocks, Types of Rocks; Directorate General of Hydrocarbons, National Data Repository, Kutch Basin, Geological Setting and Stratigraphy. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
